shots.engineer: Here is a small reporting system. A queue hands out jobs such as rebuild report forty-two. Two workers, on two different machines, take jobs from it, and both read and write the same report store. Queues often deliver a job more than once, and a user can press the button twice. So sooner or later, both workers pick up the same report at the same moment.
shots.executive: Two workers on separate machines can end up doing the same job on the same report at the same time.

shots.title: Lost update
shots.engineer: Watch what happens. Both workers get the job. Both read version one of the report. Worker A builds its version two and writes it. Worker B, working from the same old version one, writes its own version two straight over the top. A's work is gone, and nobody gets an error. Swap the report for an account balance or a file, and the result is a lost payment or a corrupted file.
shots.executive: Both read the same starting point and the second write silently erases the first. Nobody sees an error, but data is lost.

shots.title: Local mutex
shots.engineer: The obvious fix is a lock around the update, the same mutex we would use between threads. But a mutex lives in one process's memory. Worker A locks its mutex and is granted it. Worker B locks its own mutex, on another machine, and is granted that too. Neither lock knows the other exists, so both write and B still overwrites A. To exclude another machine, the lock has to live somewhere both machines can see.
shots.executive: A lock inside one program cannot stop a program on another machine. The lock has to be shared.

shots.title: Acquire and release
shots.engineer: A distributed lock lives in a shared service. It has three parts. A lock key, named after the resource, whose value says who owns it: a random string only that worker knows. A lease, so the key expires on its own and a crashed holder cannot block everyone for ever. And, for correctness, a fencing counter, which we will come back to. Worker A acquires the key if it is free; B is told it is held and retries. A releases it, but only if the value is still its own.
shots.executive: Workers ask a shared service for the lock. It records who holds it and for how long, so a crashed worker's lock eventually frees itself.

shots.title: Redis
shots.engineer: With Redis, step by step. Worker A sends SET, with the lock key, its random value, NX meaning only if the key does not exist, and PX thirty thousand: expire in thirty seconds. Redis says OK. B sends the same command and gets nil, so it waits a random delay and tries again. A does its work, then releases with a small script: delete the key only if the value is still a-7f3. B's retry now succeeds.
shots.executive: One command sets the lock only if nobody has it, with a thirty-second expiry. The holder removes it when finished, but only if it is still theirs.

card.heading: Why each part matters
points: Without | What goes wrong
NX | Everyone "acquires" by overwriting the key
An expiry | A crashed holder blocks the resource for ever
A random owner value | A slow holder deletes the next holder's lock
Setting both in one command | A crash between them leaves a lock that never expires

shots.engineer: Each piece earns its place. Without NX, every worker simply overwrites the key and believes it won. Without an expiry, a holder that crashes keeps the lock for ever. Without the random value, a slow holder whose lease has run out would delete the lock that now belongs to someone else; Redis's own documentation gives exactly this reason. And the value and expiry are set in one atomic command, so there is no moment where the lock exists with no expiry.
shots.executive: Only-if-free, an expiry, and a private owner value each close a specific hole. Leave any one out and two workers can collide.

shots.title: Paused holder
shots.engineer: Now the hard case, described by Martin Kleppmann. A holds the lock with a thirty second lease, then stops for forty seconds: a long garbage collection pause, or a stalled virtual machine. The lease expires and B is granted the lock. B writes the report. A wakes up, still believing it holds the lock, and writes over B. Its release then finds a different value and deletes nothing. The owner value protected the lock, but not the data.
shots.executive: If the holder freezes longer than its lease, someone else gets the lock, and the frozen worker wakes up and overwrites their work anyway.

shots.title: Fencing token
shots.engineer: The fix is a fencing token. Every time the lock is granted, the service hands out a number that only goes up. A gets thirty-three; after the lease expires, B gets thirty-four. Every write carries its token, and the store remembers the highest it has seen. B's write with thirty-four succeeds. A's late write with thirty-three is rejected. The check happens at the resource, which is the only place that can see the order. Google's Chubby called these sequencers.
shots.executive: Each lock grant gets a rising number, and the data store refuses any write carrying an older number than one it has already seen.

card.heading: Other ways two holders appear
points: Primary fails before replicating the key; the replica grants it again
A clock jump makes a key expire early
A lock node restarts without the key on disk
Work outlives the lease: renew it, or keep work short

shots.engineer: A pause is not the only way to get two holders. Redis replication is asynchronous, so a primary can grant the lock and crash before the replica has the key; the promoted replica grants it again. Redis expiry uses the wall clock, so a clock jump can end a lease early. A node that restarts without the key on disk forgets the lock. And work that outlives the lease must renew it, or stay short.
shots.executive: Failovers, clock changes and restarts can all hand the same lock to two workers. The lock alone cannot promise exclusivity.

card.heading: Two kinds of lock
points: Efficiency lock | Correctness lock
Avoids doing work twice | Prevents corruption or data loss
A rare duplicate is fine | A duplicate is an incident
Single Redis node is enough | Consensus store: ZooKeeper, etcd
No fencing needed | Fencing tokens checked by the resource

shots.engineer: Kleppmann's key distinction is why you want the lock. An efficiency lock stops you doing work twice, such as sending the same email or rebuilding a report. If it occasionally fails, you waste a little effort, so one Redis node is fine. A correctness lock protects data, and a failure means corruption. Then you need a consensus-backed store such as ZooKeeper or etcd, and fencing tokens checked by the resource itself.
shots.executive: Decide first whether a rare duplicate is merely wasteful or actually harmful. Harmful needs a stronger, more expensive lock with an extra safety check.

card.heading: Redlock and the debate
points: Redlock says | Critics reply
Lock a majority of 5 independent masters | Still no fencing token
Subtract elapsed time from the validity | Assumes bounded pauses and clock drift
Survives some nodes failing | Too heavy for efficiency, too weak for correctness

shots.engineer: Redlock is Redis's answer to the failover problem: run five independent masters, set the key on all of them, and count the lock as held only on a majority within the validity time. Kleppmann argued in 2016 that it still offers no fencing token and relies on timing assumptions. Antirez, Redis's creator, replied in Is Redlock safe?, accepting the point about monotonic clocks but disputing the rest. Redis's own page now links both and recommends fencing tokens.
shots.executive: Redis offers a multi-server lock called Redlock. Experts disagree on whether it is safe enough to protect data, so use it to save effort rather than to guarantee correctness.

card.heading: Often you need no lock at all
points: Alternative | Use when
Version column, compare-and-set | Conflicts are rare; retry on mismatch
SELECT … FOR UPDATE | The data sits in one database
PostgreSQL advisory lock | One database, application-defined resource
Idempotent operations | Running twice can be made harmless

shots.engineer: Before reaching for a lock service, ask whether you need one. Optimistic concurrency adds a version column: update where version is still one, and retry if no row changed. If the data sits in one database, a row lock with select for update, or a PostgreSQL advisory lock, uses the database you already trust. And if the operation can be made idempotent, a duplicate stops mattering.
shots.executive: Often the database can prevent the conflict itself, or the work can be made safe to repeat. Then no separate lock service is needed.

shots.title: Lineage
shots.engineer: In the wild. Redis documents the single-node SET pattern and Redlock, which runs the same SET across independent masters. Martin Kleppmann's 2016 article criticised Redlock, citing Google's Chubby paper from 2006 for the efficiency versus correctness split. Antirez replied. Kleppmann recommends a consensus system such as ZooKeeper, whose lock recipe uses ephemeral sequential nodes, with the zxid as a fencing token. etcd offers a mutex tied to a session lease. PostgreSQL has advisory locks.
shots.executive: Redis, ZooKeeper, etcd and PostgreSQL all offer locks. Google's Chubby showed the idea at scale, and a public debate shaped how people use Redis locks.

shots.title: Neighbours
shots.engineer: Its neighbours. Leader election is the same machinery, held indefinitely to be in charge rather than briefly for one operation. A timeout is what frees a dead holder; a lease is a timeout on ownership. Optimistic concurrency and database locks often replace a distributed lock outright. Idempotency is the backstop when two holders slip through. And two-phase commit holds locks on several resources while it waits for everyone to agree.
shots.executive: Locks are close cousins of leader election, rely on timeouts, and are often replaced by database features or by making work safe to repeat.

card.heading: Recap
points: Share the lock, own it with a secret, and let it expire
A lease can end while the holder still thinks it owns it
For correctness, fence at the resource, or avoid the lock

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. A lock must live where every machine can see it, carry a value only the owner knows, and expire on its own. A lease can run out while the holder still believes it owns the lock, so the lock alone never guarantees one writer. And when correctness matters, make the resource check fencing tokens, or design the lock away with versions and idempotency.
shots.executive: Share the lock and let it expire. Remember it can be lost without the holder knowing. When data is at stake, have the data store do the final check.

meta.blurb: One worker at a time across machines: an owned, expiring lock, and fencing tokens when correctness is at stake.
